# Appendix: Proofs {#sec-appendix .appendix}

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-moments] {#sec-proof-moments}

<!-- MODIFIED: added λ computations -->
For the binary distribution, the moments follow directly from the definition:

$$
\kappa^B=\frac{1}{2u_\ell}+\frac{1}{2u_H},
\qquad
\nu^B=\frac{u_\ell+u_H}{2},
\qquad
\lambda^B=\frac{1}{2u_\ell^2}+\frac{1}{2u_H^2}.
$$

For the uniform distribution, let the density be

$$
f(v)=\frac{1}{2\delta}\mathbf{1}_{[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]}(v).
$$

Because $[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]\subset(0,\infty)$ is compact and $v\mapsto v^{-1/2}$ is continuous on it, $v^{-1/2}$ is Lebesgue integrable. Let $u=\sqrt v$; this is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, with $dv=2u\,du$. Hence

$$
\kappa^U
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}v^{-1/2}\,dv
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\cdot\bigl[2\sqrt v\bigr]_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}
=\frac{u_H-u_\ell}{\delta}.
$$

Similarly, $v\mapsto v^{1/2}$ is also Lebesgue integrable, so

$$
\nu^U
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}v^{1/2}\,dv
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\cdot\left[\frac{2}{3}v^{3/2}\right]_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}
=\frac{u_H^3-u_\ell^3}{3\delta}.
$$

For $\lambda^U$, observe that $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ is integrable on the compact set $(0,\infty)\supset[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]$:

$$
\lambda^U
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\int_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}v^{-1}\,dv
=\frac{1}{2\delta}\cdot\bigl[\ln v\bigr]_{\mu-\delta}^{\mu+\delta}
=\frac{\ln(\mu+\delta)-\ln(\mu-\delta)}{2\delta}
=\frac{\ln(u_H^2/u_\ell^2)}{2\delta}
=\frac{\ln(u_H/u_\ell)}{\delta}.
$$

To compare $\kappa^B$ and $\kappa^U$, note first that $v\mapsto v^{-1/2}$ is strictly convex on $(0,\infty)$. Jensen's inequality therefore implies

$$
\kappa^B=\E_{\mathrm{binary}}[V_L^{-1/2}]
>
\left(\E_{\mathrm{binary}}[V_L]\right)^{-1/2}
=\mu^{-1/2}.
$$

Moreover, since $u_H^2-u_\ell^2=2\delta$,

$$
\kappa^U=\frac{u_H-u_\ell}{\delta}=\frac{2}{u_H+u_\ell},
\qquad
\kappa^B=\frac{1}{2u_\ell}+\frac{1}{2u_H}
=\frac{u_H+u_\ell}{2u_\ell u_H}.
$$

Hence

$$
\kappa^B-\kappa^U
=\frac{(u_H+u_\ell)^2-4u_\ell u_H}{2u_\ell u_H(u_H+u_\ell)}
=\frac{(u_H-u_\ell)^2}{2u_\ell u_H(u_H+u_\ell)}
>0.
$$

Therefore $\kappa^B>\kappa^U$.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ss]

<!-- MODIFIED: completely rewritten to derive the correct BNE; previous proof solved the Stackelberg leader problem by substituting labor's BR into management's objective -->

We seek a Bayesian Nash equilibrium $(x_M^*,\,x_L^*(\cdot))$ in which management chooses a constant $x_M^*$ and labor responds type-by-type. By @eq-brl, labor's best response to $x_M^*$ for type $v$ is

$$
x_L^*(v)=\sqrt{vx_M^*}-x_M^*.
$$

For management, given that labor uses the equilibrium strategy, management's first-order condition is obtained by differentiating $\E[U_M(x_L^*(V_L),x_M;V)]$ with respect to $x_M$:

$$
V\cdot\E\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_M}\frac{x_M}{x_L^*(V_L)+x_M}\right]=1.
$$

Since $x_L^*(v)+x_M = \sqrt{vx_M}$, the partial derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_M}\frac{x_M}{\sqrt{vx_M}}
=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_M}\frac{\sqrt{x_M}}{\sqrt{v}}
=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{vx_M}}.
$$

Wait—management's payoff function, written out explicitly, is

$$
U_M(x_L,x_M;V)=\frac{x_M}{x_L+x_M}V-x_M.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $x_M$ (holding $x_L$ fixed):

$$
\frac{\partial U_M}{\partial x_M}=\frac{x_L}{(x_L+x_M)^2}V-1.
$$

At the equilibrium, $x_L=x_L^*(v)=\sqrt{vx_M^*}-x_M^*$ and $x_L+x_M^*=\sqrt{vx_M^*}$, so $x_L/(x_L+x_M^*)^2 = (\sqrt{vx_M^*}-x_M^*)/(vx_M^*)$. Management's FOC, taking expectation over types, is

$$
V\cdot\E\!\left[\frac{\sqrt{V_Lx_M^*}-x_M^*}{V_Lx_M^*}\right]=1.
$$

Simplifying the expectation:

$$
V\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x_M^*}}\E\!\left[V_L^{-1/2}\right]-\E\!\left[V_L^{-1}\right]\right)
=V\!\left(\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{x_M^*}}-\lambda\right)=1,
$$

where $\lambda\equiv\E[V_L^{-1}]$. Solving for $\sqrt{x_M^*}$:

$$
\sqrt{x_M^*}=\frac{V\kappa}{1+V\lambda},
\qquad
x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}.
$$

The second-order condition for management is

$$
-V\cdot\E\!\left[\frac{x_L^*(V_L)}{(x_L^*(V_L)+x_M)^{3/2}}\right]\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x_M}}<0,
$$

which holds because $x_L^*(v)\ge 0$. Hence $x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}$ is the unique equilibrium management effort.

Substituting into @eq-brl,

$$
x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\frac{V\kappa\sqrt{v}}{1+V\lambda}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}.
$$

The total $x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)+x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}=V\kappa\sqrt{v}/(1+V\lambda)$. Substituting into @eq-ul and @eq-um:

$$
U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\frac{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)}{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)+x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}v - x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\left(1-\frac{V\kappa}{(1+V\lambda)\sqrt{v}}\right)v - \left(\frac{V\kappa\sqrt{v}}{1+V\lambda}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}\right)
=\left(\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{1+V\lambda}\right)^2,
$$

$$
U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)
=\frac{x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}{x_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)+x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}}V - x_M^{\mathrm{SS}}
=\frac{V\kappa}{(1+V\lambda)\sqrt{v}}\cdot V - \frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}
=\frac{V^2\kappa}{(1+V\lambda)\sqrt{v}}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}.
$$

Taking expectations:

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\E\!\left[v-\frac{2V\kappa\sqrt{v}}{1+V\lambda}+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}\right]
=\mu-\frac{2V\kappa\nu}{1+V\lambda}+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2},
$$

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\frac{V^2\kappa}{1+V\lambda}\E[V_L^{-1/2}]-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}
=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{1+V\lambda}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}
=\frac{V^3\kappa^2\lambda}{(1+V\lambda)^2}. \qquad\square
$$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ml]

<!-- MODIFIED: ML payoffs are now distinct from SS; they match the old (incorrect) SS formula -->
In ML, management commits first. Labor observes $x_M$ and best-responds type-by-type with $x_L^*(x_M;v)=\sqrt{vx_M}-x_M$, which management anticipates. Management therefore maximizes

$$
\E\!\left[U_M(x_L^*(V_L),x_M;V)\right]
=\E\!\left[V\sqrt{\frac{x_M}{V_L}}-x_M\right]
=V\sqrt{x_M}\,\kappa-x_M.
$$

This is the Stackelberg leader objective. The first- and second-order conditions are

$$
\frac{V\kappa}{2\sqrt{x_M}}-1=0,
\qquad
-\frac{V\kappa}{4x_M^{3/2}}<0,
$$

giving the unique maximizer $x_M^{\mathrm{ML}}=V^2\kappa^2/4$. Then @eq-brl implies

$$
x_L^{\mathrm{ML}}(v)=\frac{V\kappa}{2}\sqrt{v}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4},
\qquad
x_L^{\mathrm{ML}}(v)+x_M^{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{V\kappa}{2}\sqrt{v}.
$$

Substituting into @eq-ul and @eq-um:

$$
U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}(v)=\left(\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right)^2,
\qquad
U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}(v)=\frac{V^2\kappa}{2\sqrt{v}}-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}.
$$

Taking expectations:

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]=\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4},
\qquad
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]=\frac{V^2\kappa}{2}\cdot\kappa-\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}.
$$

Note the difference from the corrected SS: $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]=V^2\kappa^2/4$ while $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]=V^3\kappa^2\lambda/(1+V\lambda)^2$. They differ unless $V\lambda=1$. $\square$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-separating]

Labor solves

$$
\max_{x_L\ge 0}\;W(x_L;v)=\max_{x_L\ge 0}\left(\frac{v}{\sqrt V}\sqrt{x_L}-x_L\right).
$$

The first-order condition is

$$
\frac{v}{2\sqrt{Vx_L}} - 1 = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
x_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

The second-order condition is

$$
\frac{\partial^2 W}{\partial x_L^2}=-\frac{v}{4\sqrt V}x_L^{-3/2}<0,
$$

so this is the unique global optimum. Then @eq-brm implies

$$
x_M^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)
=\sqrt{V\cdot\frac{v^2}{4V}}-\frac{v^2}{4V}
=\frac{v(2V-v)}{4V}.
$$

Substituting into @eq-ul and @eq-um yields @eq-ul-lm and @eq-um-lm.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-no-pool]

The proof has two steps.

First, show that equilibrium effort is one-to-one in type. Define

$$
\phi:[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]\to\mathbb{R},
\qquad
\phi(v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

Because $\mu>\delta>0$, the support $[\mu-\delta,\mu+\delta]$ lies in $(0,\infty)$. Hence, for every $v$ in the support,

$$
\phi'(v)=\frac{v}{2V}>0.
$$

Therefore $\phi$ is strictly increasing on the support and thus injective. Equivalently, if $v\neq v'$, then

$$
\phi(v)\neq \phi(v').
$$

So distinct types cannot share the same optimal effort. Any candidate strategy that assigns the same effort to two different types is incompatible with the injectivity of $\phi$.

Second, prove strict global incentive compatibility of truthful play. Fix any true type $v$ and any $s\neq v$. If type $v$ chooses the effort associated with type $s$,

$$
x_L=\frac{s^2}{4V},
$$

then, after management responds according to @eq-brm, type $v$ obtains

$$
\tilde{U}(v,s)
=\frac{v}{\sqrt{V}}\cdot\frac{s}{2\sqrt{V}}-\frac{s^2}{4V}
=\frac{2vs-s^2}{4V}.
$$

Truthful play yields

$$
U(v,v)=\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

The payoff difference is

$$
U(v,v)-\tilde{U}(v,s)
=\frac{v^2-2vs+s^2}{4V}
=\frac{(v-s)^2}{4V}>0
\qquad\forall s\neq v.
$$

This difference is a positive-definite quadratic form and is strictly positive for every $s\neq v$. Hence any strategy that asks type $v$ to choose $s^2/(4V)$ with $s\neq v$ is strictly dominated by truthful play.

In the binary-type special case, this condition corresponds exactly to the main-text constraints `IC_H` and `IC_L`. Those two constraints jointly are necessary and sufficient for the separating candidate to be feasible. Necessity follows because a separating equilibrium must rule out imitation in both directions. Sufficiency follows because, given the continuation best response in @eq-brm, once both IC constraints hold, each type optimally chooses its own action.

Let

$$
D(v,s)\equiv U(v,v)-\tilde U(v,s)=\frac{(v-s)^2}{4V}.
$$

For fixed $s$, $D(v,s)$ is zero only at $v=s$, and

$$
\frac{\partial D(v,s)}{\partial v}=\frac{v-s}{2V}
$$

changes sign at that point. This gives the single-crossing representation. But no separate single-crossing argument is needed here, because $D(v,s)>0$ for every $s\neq v$ already delivers the stronger global strict IC result.

Because management's continuation best response depends only on observed effort and the parameter $V$, not on posterior beliefs, beliefs cannot overturn this deviation argument. Therefore no pooling or semi-separating behavior can arise in PBE, and there is no parameter region in which pooling is feasible. The LM subgame admits a unique PBE, and it is separating.

## Proof of the LM Expected-Payoff Formulas

From @eq-ul-lm, $U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)=v^2/(4V)$, so

$$
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E\!\left[\frac{V_L^2}{4V}\right]
=\frac{\E[V_L^2]}{4V}
=\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$

From @eq-um-lm,

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E\!\left[\frac{(2V-V_L)^2}{4V}\right]
=\frac{4V^2-4V\E[V_L]+\E[V_L^2]}{4V}
=\frac{4V^2-4V\mu+\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$ $\square$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-stage1-br]

<!-- MODIFIED: point 3 added to reflect that M always prefers F when L plays S -->
From the stage-1 payoff matrix:

- If management chooses S, labor compares $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ from F with $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ from S; the difference is $\Delta_L$.
- If management chooses F, labor compares $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ from F with $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]$ from S.
- If labor chooses F, management compares $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ from F with $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ from S; the difference is $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]-\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$.
- If labor chooses S, management compares $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]$ from F with $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ from S; by the Key Lemma this difference is $V^2\kappa^2(1-V\lambda)^2/(4(1+V\lambda)^2)\ge 0$, so management (weakly) prefers F.

Parts 1 and 2 of the proposition follow from the first two bullet points. Part 3 follows from the last bullet point: management's unique best response when labor plays S is F (strictly so when $V\lambda\ne 1$).

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-stage1-ne]

<!-- MODIFIED: updated to reflect corrected SS ≠ ML; (S,S) is never NE -->
Inspect each cell of the stage-1 payoff matrix:

- At $(S,F)$: if labor deviates from S to F, the outcome changes from ML to SS; labor has no incentive iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\le 0$. If management deviates from F to S, the outcome changes from ML to SS; by the Key Lemma, $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, so management never deviates. Hence $(S,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$.

- At $(F,F)$: if labor deviates from F to S, the outcome changes from SS to ML; labor has no incentive iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\le 0$. If management deviates from F to S, the outcome changes from SS to LM; management has no incentive iff $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_M'\ge 0$. Hence $(F,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$ and $\Delta_M'\ge 0$.

- At $(S,S)$: management compares $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]$ (deviate to F) with $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ (stay at S). By the Key Lemma, $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, so management always deviates. Hence $(S,S)$ is never a Nash equilibrium.

- At $(F,S)$: labor prefers F to S iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\ge 0$. Management prefers S to F iff $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$. Note that $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ does not simplify directly to $\Delta_M\le 0$; however, since $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, the condition $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ is implied whenever $\Delta_M\le 0$. Hence $(F,S)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\ge 0$ and $\Delta_M\le 0$.

This proves the proposition. $\square$

## Proof of Theorem [-@thm-timing-eq]

<!-- MODIFIED: rewritten; Key Lemma proved first; ML no longer always NE; (S,S) never NE -->

**Key Lemma.**

$$
\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]-\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}-\frac{V^3\kappa^2\lambda}{(1+V\lambda)^2}
=V^2\kappa^2\!\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{V\lambda}{(1+V\lambda)^2}\right)
=V^2\kappa^2\cdot\frac{(1+V\lambda)^2-4V\lambda}{4(1+V\lambda)^2}
=V^2\kappa^2\cdot\frac{(1-V\lambda)^2}{4(1+V\lambda)^2}\;\ge\;0,
$$

with equality iff $V\lambda=1$. This proves the Key Lemma.

**Part 4: $(S,S)$ is never a Nash equilibrium.** At $(S,S)$, management can deviate from S to F, changing the outcome from SS to ML. The gain is $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]-\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge 0$. Management therefore weakly prefers to deviate (strictly so when $V\lambda\ne 1$). Hence $(S,S)$ is never a Nash equilibrium.

**Part 1: $(S,F)$ (ML) is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$.**

- Management at $(S,F)$: deviating from F to S changes the outcome from ML to SS. The gain $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]-\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\le 0$ by the Key Lemma. Management never deviates.
- Labor at $(S,F)$: deviating from S to F changes the outcome from ML to SS. Labor does not deviate iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\le 0$.

Hence $(S,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$.

**Part 2: $(F,S)$ (LM) is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\ge 0$ and $\Delta_M\le 0$.**

- Labor at $(F,S)$: deviating from F to S changes the outcome from LM to SS. Labor does not deviate iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\ge 0$.
- Management at $(F,S)$: deviating from S to F changes the outcome from LM to SS. Management does not deviate iff $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$. Since $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]$ (Key Lemma), this condition is implied by $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_M\le 0$.

Hence $(F,S)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\ge 0$ and $\Delta_M\le 0$. Substituting @eq-delta-l and @eq-delta-m yields the explicit inequalities in the theorem.

**Part 3: $(F,F)$ (SS) is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$ and $\Delta_M'\ge 0$.**

- Labor at $(F,F)$: deviating from F to S changes the outcome from SS to ML. Labor does not deviate iff $\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_L\le 0$.
- Management at $(F,F)$: deviating from F to S changes the outcome from SS to LM. Management does not deviate iff $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$, i.e., $\Delta_M'\ge 0$.

Hence $(F,F)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff $\Delta_L\le 0$ and $\Delta_M'\ge 0$. $\square$

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-ex-ante-decomp]

Starting from $R(v)\equiv U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}(v)-U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}(v)$ and taking expectation over $V_L$,

$$
\E[R(V_L)]
=
\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]-\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=
-\Delta_L.
$$

This proves the proposition.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-exact-condition]

Type $v$ ex post prefers to move first if and only if

$$
R(v)\le 0.
$$

By definition,

$$
R(v)\leq 0
\iff
\left(\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right)^2\leq\frac{v^2}{4V}.
$$

Because $v>0$, the square root of the right-hand side, $\frac{v}{2\sqrt V}$, is strictly positive. Hence the preceding inequality is equivalent to

$$
\left|\sqrt{v}-\frac{V\kappa}{2}\right|
\leq
\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}.
$$

Expanding the absolute-value inequality gives the double inequality

$$
\sqrt{v}-\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}
\leq
\frac{V\kappa}{2}
\leq
\sqrt{v}+\frac{v}{2\sqrt{V}}.
$$

This proves the proposition.

## Proof of Proposition [-@prp-mgmt]

<!-- MODIFIED: updated LM formula notation -->
From @eq-eum-ml and @eq-eum-lm,

$$
\E\!\left[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}\right]=\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4},
\qquad
\E\!\left[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}\right]=\frac{(2V-\mu)^2+\sigma^2}{4V}.
$$

Therefore the condition $\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]\ge\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]$ is exactly @eq-mgmt-cond. Note that Theorem [-@thm-timing-eq] requires $\Delta_M \le 0$ for LM to be an equilibrium, so the inequality is reversed there.

## Proof of the Welfare Formulas in Section @sec-welfare

<!-- MODIFIED: SS and ML now have distinct welfare; separate formulas provided -->
By definition, $W=U_L+U_M$.

For SS (corrected BNE):

$$
\E[W^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\E[U_L^{\mathrm{SS}}]+\E[U_M^{\mathrm{SS}}]
=\left(\mu-\frac{2V\kappa\nu}{1+V\lambda}+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{(1+V\lambda)^2}\right)
+\frac{V^3\kappa^2\lambda}{(1+V\lambda)^2}.
$$

For ML:

$$
\E[W^{\mathrm{ML}}]
=\E[U_L^{\mathrm{ML}}]+\E[U_M^{\mathrm{ML}}]
=\left(\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}\right)+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{4}
=\mu-V\kappa\nu+\frac{V^2\kappa^2}{2}.
$$

For LM:

$$
\E[W^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\E[U_L^{\mathrm{LM}}]+\E[U_M^{\mathrm{LM}}]
=\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{4V}+\frac{(2V-\mu)^2+\sigma^2}{4V}
=V-\mu+\frac{\mu^2+\sigma^2}{2V}. \qquad\square
$$
